chain.aiLabel: How much AI changes its work

aiUses.what: Designing and screening molecules on a computer before the lab makes them.
aiUses.why: A faster hit means more years of patent life left at launch; the AI lab is paid milestones, not the drug's sales. No AI-discovered drug has been approved yet.

aiUses.what: Picking trial sites, finding eligible patients and cleaning trial data.
aiUses.why: Months saved on a trial are months of patent sales. IQVIA owns the patient data the AI runs on, which rivals cannot copy.

aiUses.what: Faster MRI scans, cleaner images, and flagging which scan a radiologist should read first.
aiUses.why: Sold bundled with the machine and its service contract, so it defends the installed base rather than earning separately.

aiUses.what: Listening to the visit and writing the note, the inbox reply and the billing codes.
aiUses.why: Every AI scribe has to write into the record system, and Epic now builds its own. The record is the toll booth.

aiUses.what: Approving, pricing and denying claims and prior authorisations at speed.
aiUses.why: Contested: lawsuits over automated denials and new state rules limit how far it can go.

columns.name: Materials & parts
columns.what: What the factories consume: the active ingredients in pills (mostly made in India and China), the glass vials and pens injectables are filled into, and the helium and electronics inside scanners.

columns.name: Tools
columns.what: The equipment and consumables biologic drugs are grown and purified with, and the gene sequencers research runs on. Sold to every drug maker and contract factory, whichever drug wins.

columns.name: Discovery & trials
columns.what: Where drugs are found and proven: AI drug-discovery labs, and the contract research firms that run lab tests and clinical trials for drug makers.

columns.name: Contract factories
columns.what: Factories that make drugs and devices for someone else's brand. An approved biologics plant takes three to five years to build and qualify.

columns.name: Makers
columns.what: The companies whose name is on the product: drug makers in the top band, device makers in the middle. Patents make most of the money here.

columns.name: Middlemen
columns.what: The three wholesalers that move nearly every US prescription, and the pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) that decide which drugs an insurance plan covers and collect rebates for it.

columns.name: Hospitals & doctors
columns.what: Where care happens, and the record system it is written into. The Thai branch sits at the bottom.

columns.name: Insurers
columns.what: Who manages the bill. In the US the biggest insurers also own a PBM and doctors' groups, so one company can sit on both sides of a payment.

columns.name: Who pays
columns.what: Where the money starts: government programmes, employers, and patients themselves.

ai.note: Uses AI in its diagnostics and glucose data apps.

moat.breaks: GLP-1 drugs may reduce some device demand; Dexcom competes.
moat.holds: Scale manufacturing of sensors and broad diagnostics.
moat.line: Libre is the most-used continuous glucose monitor.

abbott.name: Abbott Laboratories
abbott.what: Diagnostics, heart devices and the FreeStyle Libre glucose sensor.

ai.note: Uses AI in discovery.

moat.breaks: Oral IL-23 pills (J&J's Icotyde) and TL1A drugs challenge injectables.
moat.holds: Patents and settlements keep Rinvoq generics out until 2037.
moat.line: Replaced Humira's sales with Skyrizi and Rinvoq within three years.

abbvie.name: AbbVie
abbvie.what: US drug maker: immunology (Skyrizi, Rinvoq, Humira), cancer, Botox.

ai.note: The whole point: AI designs and screens molecules before the lab does.

moat.breaks: No Isomorphic drug has reached human trials results yet; a tiny part of Alphabet.
moat.holds: DeepMind's models and compute, plus partnerships with Eli Lilly and Novartis.
moat.line: AlphaFold made Isomorphic the best-known AI drug-discovery lab.

alphabet.name: Alphabet
alphabet.what: On this chain only through Isomorphic Labs, its AI drug-discovery company spun out of Google DeepMind (AlphaFold).

ai.note: Uses AI in discovery and trials.

moat.breaks: Farxiga and older drugs losing exclusivity; China exposure.
moat.holds: Patents and partnerships (Daiichi Sankyo on Enhertu and Datroway).
moat.line: One of the deepest cancer pipelines.

astrazeneca.name: AstraZeneca
astrazeneca.what: Anglo-Swedish drug maker: cancer (Tagrisso, Enhertu, Calquence), diabetes and heart (Farxiga).

ai.note: Early AI use in imaging and records.

moat.breaks: Thai economy, Middle East patient flows, and price competition.
moat.holds: Brand, network and specialist centres; founded and controlled by the Prasarttong-Osoth family, which also controls Bangkok Airways.
moat.line: Over a quarter of revenue from foreign patients and a network nobody in Thailand matches.

bdms.name: Bangkok Dusit Medical Services
bdms.what: Thailand's largest private hospital group (Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej, BNH and more).

ai.note: Little disclosed.

moat.breaks: Depends on Middle East and Myanmar patients; one hospital.
moat.holds: International brand and accreditation built over decades.
moat.line: One of Asia's best-known hospitals for medical tourists.

bh.name: Bumrungrad International Hospital
bh.what: Bangkok hospital where about two-thirds of revenue comes from foreign patients.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Lowest margin of the three; lost a large customer in 2024.
moat.holds: Scale.
moat.line: One of the Big Three wholesalers.

cardinal.name: Cardinal Health
cardinal.what: US drug wholesaler and medical products maker.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Customer concentration.
moat.holds: Same scale moat as McKesson.
moat.line: One of the Big Three wholesalers.

cencora.name: Cencora
cencora.what: US drug wholesaler (formerly AmerisourceBergen); Walgreens is its biggest customer.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Depends on government rates and subsidies.
moat.holds: State contracts.
moat.line: Scale in government programmes.

centene.name: Centene
centene.what: The largest Medicaid insurer and a big Obamacare-exchange insurer.

ai.note: AI in claims review (sued over automated denials).

moat.breaks: PBM reform and rebate pass-through rules; the FTC's case against PBM insulin practices.
moat.holds: Scale in negotiating drug rebates.
moat.line: Express Scripts processes about a third of US prescription claims.

cigna.name: Cigna Group
cigna.what: Owns Express Scripts, the largest PBM, and Cigna Healthcare insurance.

ai.note: AI and computer models are the threat: they could replace some animal studies.

moat.breaks: The FDA's 2025 plan to phase down animal testing, in favour of AI models and lab-grown tissue, targets its core work.
moat.holds: Regulators require these studies, and few firms can run them at scale.
moat.line: The leading outsourced pre-clinical lab.

crl.name: Charles River Laboratories
crl.what: Runs the lab and animal studies every drug needs before human trials.

ai.note: AI in claims and customer service.

moat.breaks: PBM reform in Congress, falling pharmacy margins, and Medicare Advantage costs.
moat.holds: Integration: it earns on the same prescription three times.
moat.line: Owns the pharmacy counter, the PBM and the insurer.

cvs.name: CVS Health
cvs.what: Pharmacies, the Caremark PBM and Aetna insurance under one roof.

ai.note: Cytiva and its diagnostics units use AI in process control and lab automation.

moat.breaks: New drugs can be designed around rivals (Sartorius, Merck KGaA); customers stock up and cut orders in cycles.
moat.holds: A biologic's manufacturing process is part of its approval; swapping a supplier means revalidation.
moat.line: Cytiva's filters and resins are written into the approved recipe of many biologic drugs.

danaher.name: Danaher
danaher.what: Owns Cytiva, a leading supplier of the equipment and single-use bags biologic drugs are grown and purified in, plus diagnostics (Cepheid, Beckman).

ai.note: Uses AI in its app to predict glucose.

moat.breaks: Abbott's lower prices; reimbursement.
moat.holds: Insulin pump integrations and doctor habits.
moat.line: A leading glucose sensor brand.

dexcom.name: Dexcom
dexcom.what: Continuous glucose monitors worn by people with diabetes.

ai.note: AI helps plan chemical routes; it does not change who wins orders.

moat.breaks: Ingredient buyers can and do qualify second sources; Chinese makers compete on price.
moat.holds: Decades of chemistry know-how and FDA-inspected plants that buyers have already qualified.
moat.line: One of the lowest-cost makers of drug ingredients, with clean regulatory inspection history.

divis.name: Divi's Laboratories
divis.what: Indian maker of active pharmaceutical ingredients: the chemical that does the work inside a pill, sold to drug makers worldwide.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Drug makers can take distribution in-house; Zuellig competes.
moat.holds: Warehouses, licences and sales teams in every Thai province.
moat.line: The main outsourced route to market for foreign drugs in Thailand.

dksh.name: DKSH
dksh.what: Swiss distributor that sells and delivers drugs for global drug makers across Asia; Thailand is its largest market.

ai.note: AI in claims and prior authorisation.

moat.breaks: Medicaid and Medicare cost pressure.
moat.holds: Brand and local hospital networks.
moat.line: Blue Cross licences in 14 states.

elevance.name: Elevance Health
elevance.what: US insurer (Anthem Blue Cross plans) with its own PBM (CarelonRx).

employers.name: Employers
employers.what: Companies buying health plans for their staff, the largest private source of money.

ai.note: Builds AI note-taking, inbox replies and coding into the record; third-party scribes must integrate.

moat.breaks: Oracle Health, government interoperability rules and antitrust suits (Particle Health).
moat.holds: Replacing a hospital's record system costs years and hundreds of millions; every app must plug into it.
moat.line: Holds about 44% of US acute-care hospitals and 57% of beds.

epic.name: Epic Systems
epic.what: Private US company that makes the electronic health record most US hospital beds run on.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Thin margins and easy switching for new products.
moat.holds: Certifications and long customer relationships.
moat.line: Regulated manufacturing at scale.

flex.name: Flex
flex.what: Contract manufacturer; builds diagnostic and medical devices for device brands.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: A small part of Fujifilm; new capacity must be filled.
moat.holds: Capital and long contracts.
moat.line: Building some of the largest new biologics plants (Denmark, North Carolina).

fujifilm.name: Fujifilm
fujifilm.what: Japanese conglomerate whose Fujifilm Diosynth unit makes biologic drugs under contract.

ai.note: AI is built into its scanners: faster MRI, cleaner CT images, flagging urgent cases.

moat.breaks: China sales slowed; Chinese scanner makers compete.
moat.holds: Installed base, service contracts and hospital relationships.
moat.line: One of three makers of most of the world's large scanners.

gehc.name: GE HealthCare
gehc.what: Makes MRI, CT, ultrasound and X-ray scanners and the dyes used in scans.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Merck's Idvynso and GSK compete; US price pressure.
moat.holds: Settlements keep Biktarvy generics out until April 2036; long-acting lenacapavir extends the franchise.
moat.line: Owns most of the HIV treatment market.

gilead.name: Gilead Sciences
gilead.what: Leader in HIV (Biktarvy, Descovy, Yeztugo) and cell therapy for cancer.

ai.note: Uses AI for nurse handoffs and scheduling with Google Cloud.

moat.breaks: Medicaid cuts and insurer pressure on prices.
moat.holds: Owning many hospitals in one city.
moat.line: Local market density lets it bargain with insurers.

hca.name: HCA Healthcare
hca.what: The largest US for-profit hospital operator, about 190 hospitals.

ai.note: AI in claims; sued over automated denials.

moat.breaks: Almost all eggs in Medicare Advantage, whose payment rates the government sets.
moat.holds: Scale in one programme.
moat.line: The second-largest Medicare Advantage insurer.

humana.name: Humana
humana.what: US insurer focused on Medicare Advantage.

ai.note: AI for site selection and data cleaning.

moat.breaks: Clients switch on price and speed; demand follows biotech funding.
moat.holds: Scale and trial-site networks.
moat.line: One of the few firms that can run global Phase 3 trials.

icon.name: ICON
icon.what: Irish contract research firm running clinical trials for drug makers.

ai.note: Sequencing data feeds AI drug discovery; it sells software for it.

moat.breaks: Cheaper rivals (Element, Ultima, MGI/Complete Genomics) have cut prices; China blacklisted it in 2025.
moat.holds: Installed machines, validated lab tests and data formats keep customers.
moat.line: The standard sequencer in research and clinical labs.

illumina.name: Illumina
illumina.what: Makes the gene sequencers most of the world's genomics runs on.

ai.note: Uses AI on its procedure data to coach surgeons.

moat.breaks: Medtronic's Hugo, J&J's Ottava and Chinese robots are arriving; hospital capital budgets.
moat.holds: Every installed robot sells instruments for years, and surgeons train on it.
moat.line: The standard soft-tissue surgical robot for two decades.

intuitive.name: Intuitive Surgical
intuitive.what: Makes the da Vinci surgical robot: about 12,000 installed, used in over 3 million operations in 2025.

ai.note: Uses its data and AI to pick trial sites and find patients faster.

moat.breaks: Biotech funding cycles; drug makers can bring trial work in-house or use cheaper rivals.
moat.holds: Data assets nobody else has at that scale, plus relationships with trial sites worldwide.
moat.line: Runs trials for most big drug makers and owns the data used to find trial patients and sell drugs.

iqvia.name: IQVIA
iqvia.what: The largest contract research firm, and owner of the biggest database of anonymised prescription and patient data.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Thin margins; brands can move work.
moat.holds: Medical device quality certification takes time to earn.
moat.line: Large, regulated factories for devices.

jabil.name: Jabil
jabil.what: Contract electronics manufacturer; builds medical devices for device brands.

ai.note: Uses AI in surgery (its Ottava robot) and discovery.

moat.breaks: Stelara lost US exclusivity in 2025; Darzalex in 2029; talc litigation.
moat.holds: Breadth across drugs and devices; strong immunology pipeline.
moat.line: Leads multiple myeloma with Darzalex and has a large device business.

jnj.name: Johnson & Johnson
jnj.what: Drugs (Darzalex, Tremfya, Stelara, Carvykti) and medical devices (orthopaedics, surgery, heart).

ai.note: Partners with Isomorphic and others on AI discovery; uses AI in trials.

moat.breaks: Price pressure from US government deals and cash-pay channels; Novo, Amgen and Roche are chasing.
moat.holds: Patents, manufacturing scale for peptides, and a pipeline of next-generation obesity drugs.
moat.line: Leads the biggest drug class in history, with patents on tirzepatide to 2036.

lilly.name: Eli Lilly
lilly.what: The largest drug maker by value: obesity and diabetes (Mounjaro, Zepbound, the Foundayo pill), cancer (Verzenio), Alzheimer's (Kisunla).

ai.note: Not relevant to its healthcare business.

moat.breaks: Healthcare is a small part of Linde; helium-free MRI magnets would remove one use.
moat.holds: Gas is costly to ship, so whoever owns the plant near the customer keeps it.
moat.line: One of three global industrial-gas majors, with long contracts and local monopolies on pipelines.

linde.name: Linde
linde.what: Industrial gases. In healthcare it supplies the helium that cools MRI magnets and medical oxygen to hospitals.

ai.note: Process analytics; not a big lever.

moat.breaks: Big drug makers are building their own plants; Samsung Biologics competes on price and speed.
moat.holds: Approved plants take years to build and qualify; a drug's process is tied to its plant.
moat.line: One of the largest makers of other companies' biologic drugs.

lonza.name: Lonza
lonza.what: Swiss contract manufacturer of biologic drugs and cell therapies.

ai.note: Logistics optimisation.

moat.breaks: Thin margins; depends on a few huge customers (CVS is its largest).
moat.holds: Scale, warehouses and contracts no new entrant can match.
moat.line: One of three wholesalers that move nearly every US prescription.

mckesson.name: McKesson
mckesson.what: The largest US drug wholesaler; also distributes medical supplies and cancer-clinic services.

medicaid.name: Medicaid
medicaid.what: State and federal programme for low-income people; mostly run through private insurers like Centene.

medicare.name: Medicare
medicare.what: The federal programme for over-65s. It pays hospitals and doctors directly, or pays private insurers a fixed amount per person under Medicare Advantage.

ai.note: Uses AI in trial operations.

moat.breaks: Depends on biotech funding; cancellations hit fast.
moat.holds: Therapeutic expertise and a reputation for execution.
moat.line: Full-service trials for biotechs without their own trial teams.

medpace.name: Medpace
medpace.what: Contract research firm focused on small and mid-sized biotechs.

ai.note: AI in imaging and colonoscopy (GI Genius).

moat.breaks: Slow growth; competitors lead in several categories.
moat.holds: Approved products and surgeon training.
moat.line: Broadest device catalogue and hospital relationships.

medtronic.name: Medtronic
medtronic.what: The largest pure medical device maker: heart, diabetes, spine, surgical robots (Hugo).

ai.note: Uses AI in discovery and trials.

moat.breaks: Keytruda's main US patent ends in 2028; the under-the-skin version (Keytruda Qlex) is its defence.
moat.holds: Patents and a decade of trial data across cancers.
moat.line: Owns Keytruda, the backbone of cancer immunotherapy.

merck.name: Merck & Co
merck.what: US drug maker (MSD outside North America). Keytruda, the best-selling cancer drug, is about half its sales.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: A conglomerate: semiconductors and its own drugs dilute the bioprocess story.
moat.holds: Same revalidation lock-in as Cytiva and Sartorius.
moat.line: Filters and reagents qualified into drug processes.

merckkgaa.name: Merck KGaA
merckkgaa.what: German science group (MilliporeSigma in the US): bioprocess filters and chemicals, plus its own drugs. Not the US Merck.

ai.note: Partners with Isomorphic Labs.

moat.breaks: Entresto lost US exclusivity in 2025; its Lp(a) drug pelacarsen failed in 2026.
moat.holds: Patents and a broad pipeline.
moat.line: Kisqali is gaining share in breast cancer.

novartis.name: Novartis
novartis.what: Swiss drug maker: breast cancer (Kisqali), heart (Entresto, Leqvio), immunology (Cosentyx).

ai.note: Uses AI in discovery and trials.

moat.breaks: Losing share to Lilly; semaglutide patents expire in some markets from 2026, and CagriSema disappointed.
moat.holds: Peptide manufacturing (it bought three Catalent fill-finish plants in 2024) and a century in diabetes.
moat.line: Invented the GLP-1 market and still sells about as much as Lilly.

novo.name: Novo Nordisk
novo.what: Danish maker of Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus (semaglutide), and insulin.

patients.name: Patients
patients.what: What people pay themselves: deductibles, co-pays and cash, now including cash-pay obesity drugs.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Scale: one hospital, competing with the big groups for the same insured patients.
moat.holds: Location and specialist centres.
moat.line: A single hospital with no wide moat.

pr9.name: Praram 9 Hospital
pr9.what: One Bangkok private hospital, mostly Thai patients and insurers.

publichosp.name: Thai public hospitals
publichosp.what: State hospitals that treat most Thais under the public schemes.

ai.note: Its business model is AI-first discovery.

moat.breaks: Clinical results so far are thin, and it burns cash.
moat.holds: Data plus automation few biotechs can afford.
moat.line: One of the largest proprietary biology datasets.

recursion.name: Recursion Pharmaceuticals
recursion.what: AI drug-discovery company that runs millions of automated cell experiments and trains models on the images.

ai.note: Partners with Recursion and NVIDIA on AI discovery.

moat.breaks: Older cancer drugs face biosimilars; its TIGIT drug failed in 2025.
moat.holds: Owns Genentech; diagnostics sit in nearly every hospital lab.
moat.line: The largest diagnostics business plus a deep drug portfolio.

roche.name: Roche
roche.what: Swiss drug and diagnostics maker: cancer, Alzheimer's (trontinemab), obesity (bought Carmot and 89bio).

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Concentrated customers; capacity is being added by rivals and by drug makers themselves.
moat.holds: Capacity and a record of passing FDA and EU inspections.
moat.line: Huge, fast-built capacity at low cost.

samsungbio.name: Samsung Biologics
samsungbio.what: Korean contract manufacturer with the world's largest single-site biologics capacity.

ai.note: Process-control software; not a large lever.

moat.breaks: Order cycles are volatile; competes directly with Cytiva and Merck KGaA.
moat.holds: Revalidation cost protects the installed base.
moat.line: Locked into approved processes the same way as Cytiva.

sartorius.name: Sartorius
sartorius.what: German supplier of bioreactors, filters and single-use bags for making biologic drugs.

ai.note: Little; demand follows injectable drug volumes such as GLP-1 pens.

moat.breaks: Plastic (polymer) syringes and rivals like Stevanato and Gerresheimer compete for new drugs.
moat.holds: Changing the container of an approved drug means new stability data and regulatory filings.
moat.line: Pharma-grade glass and prefilled syringes, qualified into drug filings that are hard to change.

schott.name: Schott Pharma
schott.what: German maker of the glass vials, syringes and cartridges injectable drugs are filled into.

ai.note: AI-Rad Companion and AI reconstruction ship with its scanners.

moat.breaks: China and lab diagnostics pressure.
moat.holds: Installed base and service.
moat.line: The largest imaging maker by revenue.

siemenshealth.name: Siemens Healthineers
siemenshealth.what: German maker of scanners, lab diagnostics and cancer radiation machines (Varian).

ai.note: Little; it rides injectable drug volumes.

moat.breaks: Capacity can be added by rivals; customers concentrate in a few GLP-1 makers.
moat.holds: Qualified into drug filings; switching containers is slow.
moat.line: A leading supplier of the glass cartridges inside injector pens.

stevanato.name: Stevanato Group
stevanato.what: Italian maker of vials, cartridges and syringes, and the machines that inspect them.

ai.note: Planning software for joint surgery.

moat.breaks: Hospital budgets; rivals' robots.
moat.holds: Robot plus implant bundle.
moat.line: Mako robot locks surgeons into Stryker implants.

stryker.name: Stryker
stryker.what: Orthopaedic implants and surgical equipment, including the Mako joint-replacement robot.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Many suppliers make similar parts for new designs.
moat.holds: Once a part is in an approved device, swapping it needs new testing.
moat.line: Designed into devices years before they ship.

te.name: TE Connectivity
te.what: Makes connectors, sensors and tiny wiring used inside medical devices, from catheters to surgical robots.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: Payer pressure; leverage.
moat.holds: Local density and surgeon partnerships.
moat.line: Surgery centres are its growth engine.

tenet.name: Tenet Healthcare
tenet.what: US hospitals and ambulatory surgery centres (USPI).

thaiins.name: Thai private insurers
thaiins.what: Health and life insurers paying private hospitals, a fast-growing source of Thai hospital revenue.

thaipatients.name: Thai patients
thaipatients.what: Thais paying private hospitals in cash or through insurance.

thaischemes.name: Thai public schemes
thaischemes.what: The 30-baht universal coverage scheme, social security for private employees, and the civil servant scheme.

ai.note: Sells AI-ready instruments and works with drug-discovery AI labs; its trials unit uses AI to pick sites.

moat.breaks: Spending on lab tools swings with biotech funding; China competition in consumables.
moat.holds: Breadth: one supplier for thousands of products, already written into customers' validated methods.
moat.line: Sells the tools nearly every lab and drug factory uses, whichever drug wins.

thermo.name: Thermo Fisher Scientific
thermo.what: The largest maker of lab equipment and consumables, plus a contract research business (PPD) and contract drug manufacturing.

tourists.name: Medical tourists
tourists.what: Foreign patients flying in, mostly from the Gulf, Myanmar, China and the US.

ai.note: Heavy AI use in claims and prior authorisation; contested in court.

moat.breaks: Medicare Advantage costs, a 2025 DOJ probe, and political pressure on vertical integration.
moat.holds: Scale and data across all of it.
moat.line: Sits on every side of the bill: insurer, PBM, doctors and data.

unitedhealth.name: UnitedHealth Group
unitedhealth.what: The largest US health insurer (UnitedHealthcare), PBM (Optum Rx) and employer of doctors (Optum Health).

ai.note: Uses AI to plan synthesis routes and lab automation at scale.

moat.breaks: The US BIOSECURE push aims to force US drug makers to move work away from Chinese contractors.
moat.holds: Speed and price nobody in the West matches, and years of qualified processes inside clients' filings.
moat.line: The largest contract chemistry operation in the world by capacity.

wuxiapptec.name: WuXi AppTec
wuxiapptec.what: Chinese contract chemistry and testing house: makes small-molecule drug ingredients and runs lab work for drug makers.

ai.note: Little.

moat.breaks: US BIOSECURE rules push Western clients away.
moat.holds: Speed of early development; many Chinese-origin drugs start here.
moat.line: Fast and cheap development of new biologics.

wuxibio.name: WuXi Biologics
wuxibio.what: Chinese contract developer and manufacturer of biologic drugs.

figures.label: US health spending, 2024
figures.note: 18% of GDP. Hospitals $1.6tn, doctors and clinics next, prescription drugs $467bn. This is the money at the right edge of the map.

flows.care: Care: from the premium or the government to the hospital and the doctor.
flows.devices: Devices: from the hospital bill to the device maker and its parts.
flows.drugs: Drugs: from the premium to the pharmacy, the wholesaler, the drug maker and its suppliers.

chain.lede: From the molecule to the hospital bill. Governments, employers and patients pay at the right. Their money passes through insurers and a handful of middlemen, then splits three ways: to drug makers and their contract factories, to device makers, and to the hospitals themselves. A Thai branch shows where Bangkok's hospitals and their foreign patients plug in.

diseases.lede: In healthcare the money is decided disease by disease. Where a drug works, whoever holds its patent collects until the patent ends. Where nothing works yet, many companies race, and most of them fail. Each lane is one disease: who owns it today, how big the prize is, and how far each challenger has got.
diseases.salesNote: 2025 sales from company filings. Non-dollar sales converted at about 2025 average rates and marked as converted.
diseases.title: Who owns each disease, and who is racing for the cure

linkKinds.buys: A purchase: money for goods or services, recognised as it is delivered.
linkKinds.contract: A signed multi-year commitment, mostly not yet delivered or paid.
linkKinds.internal: Inside one company: no money crosses a boundary, but the product does.
linkKinds.invests: Equity: money for a stake, not for a product.
linkKinds.rebate: Money flowing back up the chain: a drug maker pays a PBM for a place on its list.
linkKinds.warrant: Shares handed to a customer as it buys: equity running against the money.

moatKinds.contested: No durable edge; wins on execution this cycle.
moatKinds.cost: Makes it cheaper than anyone else can.
moatKinds.distribution: Owns the road to the customer.
moatKinds.know-how: Decades of process learning nobody can buy.
moatKinds.monopoly: The only one that can do it.
moatKinds.network: Worth more the more people use it.
moatKinds.scale: So big that a rival cannot reach the same cost or capacity.
moatKinds.switching: Customers have built on it; leaving costs more than staying.

none.label: No second source
none.what: Nobody else can do this at all today.

open.label: Open market
open.what: Buyers can switch within a purchase cycle.

slow.label: Quarters to replace
slow.what: Buyers can qualify another supplier, but it takes quarters.

years.label: Years to replace
years.what: A rival exists, but catching up or switching takes years.
